t.2.94.1: Rāma, the Rāghava, kissed him on the head and embraced him; then, taking Bharata onto his lap, he questioned him with an attentive mind.
t.2.94.2: Where, then, was your father, dear son, that you have come to the forest? For while he was still living, you ought not to have come to the forest.
t.2.94.4: Is King Daśaratha well, he who is true to his promises, the performer of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, firmly resolved upon dharma?
t.2.94.3: Alas, after so long I see Bharata, come from afar, scarcely recognizable in this wilderness. Why, my dear, have you come to the forest?
t.2.94.5: I hope, dear one, that the learned brahmin, ever devoted to dharma and of great splendor, the preceptor of the Ikṣvākus, is honored as is fitting?
t.2.94.6: My dear, I hope Kausalyā is happy, and Sumitrā, blessed with offspring? And does the noble queen Kaikayī rejoice?
t.2.94.7: Is your family priest, a man of noble birth, well disciplined and deeply learned, free from envy and ever watchful, duly honored by you?
t.2.94.8: I hope that the man appointed by you to tend the sacred fires, one who knows the ritual rules, is intelligent and upright, always informs you at the proper time of the oblation that has been offered and of the one that is yet to be offered?
t.2.94.9: Dear son, do you hold in due esteem your teacher Sudhanvan, who is accomplished in arrows and the finest missiles and well versed in the science of statecraft?
t.2.94.10: I hope, dear one, that you have appointed as your ministers men who are equal to yourself, brave, learned, masters of their senses, of noble birth, and skilled at reading unspoken signs?
t.2.94.11: For counsel, O Rāghava, is the root of victory for kings, when it is well guarded by ministers who keep secrets and are skilled in the śāstras.
t.2.94.12: I hope you do not fall under the sway of sleep, and that you wake at the proper time? And do you, in the latter part of the night, reflect on the most skillful means of securing your aims?
t.2.94.13: I hope you do not take counsel alone, nor deliberate anything with too many? I hope the counsel you have deliberated upon does not spread abroad through the kingdom?
t.2.94.14: I hope, O Rāghava, that once you have settled on an undertaking whose outlay is small but whose yield is great, you begin to carry it out at once and do not delay?
t.2.94.15: I hope those kings come to know all your undertakings only once they are well accomplished, or else when they have already taken the shape of things done, and not while they are still to be done?
t.2.94.17: Do you prefer a single wise man to a thousand fools? For in times of difficulty a wise man can bring about great good.
t.2.94.16: I hope, dear one, that what you or your ministers have deliberated in counsel is not found out by others through inferences or by piecing things together, nor by those who were never told of it.
t.2.94.18: Even if a lord of the earth keeps thousands of fools in attendance, or even tens of thousands, there is no real help to be found in them.
t.2.94.19: Even a single minister who is intelligent, brave, capable and discerning can bring a king, or one who is a king only in name, to great prosperity.
t.2.94.20: I trust that your best servants are employed only in the highest tasks, the middling ones in middling tasks, and the lowest in the lowest tasks?
t.2.94.21: Do you appoint to the highest tasks ministers who are the best, who have passed the tests of loyalty, who are pure, and who have served your father and grandfather before you?
t.2.94.24: Have you appointed as commander of the army one who is bold and heroic, steadfast and wise, pure, of noble birth, devoted to you, and skilful?
t.2.94.23: A physician skilled in stratagems, a man intent on corrupting one's servants, and a valiant man who covets sovereignty: whoever does not slay such men is himself slain.
t.2.94.22: I hope the sacrificial priests do not despise you as they would a fallen man, and that you are not scorned as one who exacts harsh levies, the way women scorn a man who lusts after them.
t.2.94.25: I hope that those chief warriors of yours, who are mighty, skilled in battle, of proven deeds and valorous, have been honoured by you with due respect?
t.2.94.26: Do you give your army its rations and wages, as is proper and due, when the time for payment has come, without delay?
t.2.94.27: For when the time for paying their rations and wages is allowed to pass, hired servants grow angry with their master and turn disloyal; that is held to be a very great evil.
t.2.94.28: Are all the sons of noble families, first and foremost, devoted to you? Do they, with steadfast minds, lay down their lives for your interests?
t.2.94.29: O Bharata, have you appointed as your envoy a learned man, a native of your own land, skilful, quick-witted and wise, one who delivers his message exactly as it was spoken?
t.2.94.30: Do you keep watch over the eighteen key officials among these, and the fifteen on your own side, by means of spies, three for each, who remain unrecognized?
t.2.94.31: O destroyer of foes, I hope you always conduct yourself without scorning as weak those enemies who have been driven out and who have come back again?
t.2.94.32: I hope, my dear son, that you do not keep company with materialist brāhmaṇas, for they are skilled only in what brings ruin; they are fools who think themselves learned.
t.2.94.33: Though the foremost treatises on dharma are at hand, those dull-witted men, each thinking himself clever, take up the science of reasoning and speak what is meaningless.
t.2.94.34: The city, dear one, that was dwelt in of old by our heroic forefathers, true to its name, with strong gates, and thronged with elephants, horses and chariots.
t.2.94.35: The city thronged by thousands of noble brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas and vaiśyas, ever devoted to their own duties, masters of their senses and of great energy.
t.2.94.36: Do you guard well Ayodhyā, ringed with palaces of many shapes and thronged with physicians, thriving and prosperous?
t.2.94.37: I trust your realm is graced with hundreds of shrines, thronged with well-settled people, and adorned with temples, water-stations and tanks?
t.2.94.38: Is that land full of joyful men and women and adorned with gatherings and festivals, its fields well ploughed, rich in cattle, and wholly free from acts of violence?
t.2.94.39: Is the countryside, O Rāghava, prosperous and delightful, free from beasts of prey, not dependent on rain alone, and does it dwell in happiness?
t.2.94.40: Are all those who live by farming and cattle-keeping dear to you, my dear? For the world, resting upon the means of livelihood, prospers in happiness.
t.2.94.42: I hope you console the women, and that they are well protected? I hope you do not place your trust in them, and that you do not speak secrets before them?
t.2.94.41: Have you provided for their support by protecting them and granting them exemptions? For a king must righteously protect all who dwell in his realm.
t.2.94.44: Are all your fortresses fully stocked with wealth, grain, weapons and water, and with machines, and likewise manned by craftsmen and archers?
t.2.94.43: Is the elephant forest well guarded, and do you take delight in your elephants? Do you, a prince, rising early each morning, always show yourself, finely adorned, to the people on the great highway?
t.2.94.45: I hope your income is ample and your expenditure smaller? I hope your treasury does not flow to unworthy recipients, O Rāghava?
t.2.94.46: Does your expenditure go toward the gods and the ancestors, toward brāhmaṇas and guests who arrive, toward warriors and toward the circles of your friends?
t.2.94.47: I trust that no honourable man of pure soul, falsely accused of the deed of a thief and not examined by those skilled in the law, is through greed thrown into bonds, though he is innocent?
t.2.94.48: O bull among men, I trust that a thief who has been caught, questioned, and seen at the time of the deed, with proof of his guilt, is not set free out of greed for wealth?
t.2.94.49: O Rāghava, do your learned ministers, free from partiality, examine the case of the rich man and of the poor man alike when either is in distress?
t.2.94.50: The tears that fall from those who are falsely accused, O Rāghava, destroy the sons and cattle of the one who governs only for his own pleasure.
t.2.94.52: Do you bow in reverence to your teachers and elders, to ascetics, gods and guests, to all the sacred shrines, and to the brāhmaṇas who have attained their goals?
t.2.94.51: Do you, O Rāghava, seek to win over the aged, the young, and the foremost physicians by these three means: by gifts, by affection, and by kind words?
t.2.94.53: I hope you do not obstruct dharma by artha, or again dharma by dharma, or both of them by kāma, through greed for pleasure?
t.2.94.54: O Bharata, best of victors, knower of the right time, do you pursue wealth, righteousness and pleasure, all three, apportioning each to its proper time?
t.2.94.55: O greatly wise one, do the brāhmaṇas, learned in the meaning of all the śāstras, wish you well, together with the citizens and the people of the countryside?
t.2.94.56: Unbelief, falsehood, anger, heedlessness, procrastination, failing to visit those who possess wisdom, sloth, and being ruled by the five senses.
t.2.94.57: Deliberating on matters alone, taking counsel with those who do not understand what is truly useful, failing to undertake what has been decided, and failing to guard the secrecy of one's counsel.
t.2.94.58: Failing to perform auspicious rites, and rising to greet everyone without distinction: do you avoid these fourteen faults of kings?
t.2.94.59: I hope, Rāghava, that you do not eat delicious food alone? I hope you share it with friends who long for it?
